paper_title: Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: Label-Free In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly construct multi-agent workflows that decompose a complex task and assign specialist agents from a pool. However, building such a workflow well remains challenging: how finely to divide the task, which agent to trust with each subtask, and when to create a new specialist are all critical decisions a workflow constructor needs to settle up front. Thus, whether each subtask succeeds remains unknown until the workflow runs. Yet, improving a workflow is costly. Locating a fault usually requires a reference answer, a graded outcome, or a trained assessor, and the fix is applied to the whole workflow through re-execution, re-search, or retraining. We propose InFlowOp, which prices every decision in one label-free cost that weighs how well an agent's competence meets what a subtask demands against how much that agent takes to run. Before execution, InFlowOp bidirectionally determines the granularity of task decomposition and agent assignment following from the cost rather than from a fixed template. During execution, InFlowOp corrects a fault with the cheapest move via the same cost that serves the workflow both as it is built and as it runs. Facing the workflow-level evaluation challenge, we introduce Braid, a benchmark whose tasks require multi-agent coordination beyond single-agent capability. Across various domains and backbones, InFlowOp outperforms single agent baselines by up to $+11.97\%$, achieving $+9.64\%$ with in-flow optimization. Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/InFlowOp/.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language models have grown from single-turn responders into agents that plan, call external tools, and interact with their environment (Schick et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023a; Shen et al., 2023). More recently, they begin to organize one another (Hong et al., 2024; Zhuge et al., 2024). Given task and pool of available specialist agents, an agent now writes the division of work itself, deciding which agent takes each part and in what order the parts run (Zhang et al., 2025b; Zhou et al., 2026; Yue et al., 2026). What such flow contributes is structure: the work is divided explicitly, each part goes to an agent suited to it, and progress accumulates step by step rather than resting on one long attempt. Yet the decisions such an agent makes are narrower than they appear. How finely the task is divided is fixed in advance, Figure 1: INFLOWOP for In-Flow Optimization. Complex tasks challenge single agents with long-context reasoning, while multi-agent systems introduce execution failures and coordination overhead. INFLOWOP optimize agent behaviors in-flow, enabling efficient collaboration at lower cost. Xuehang Guo <xguo15@wm.edu>, Haoyu Wang <haoyu@nec-labs.com>, Haifeng Chen <haifeng@nec-labs.com> 1 Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: INFLOWOP for In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization such as by template, prompt, or chosen number of steps. Where it does adapt, it adapts to the task alone (Liu et al., 2025; Madhwal et al., 2026; Su et al., 2026). What it would cost the available agents to carry out one division rather than another seldom enters. Where nothing available fits, the work is either forced onto another agent or new one is created, and neither choice is priced against the other (Zhang et al., 2025c; Wu et al., 2025; Shang et al., 2025). Once the flow runs, the evidence execution produces goes unused: identifying which step goes wrong is treated as needing reference answer, graded outcome, or trained assessor. The first two do not exist while the flow is running, and the third requires supervision the task alone cannot provide. Methods that dispense with all three optimize only once the run has finished, by replaying the completed trace to locate the failure or rerunning the whole flow for better answer (Chae et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026a; Lin et al., 2026). Meanwhile, when something goes wrong, the unit of fix is the whole flow, e.g., re-executed, re-searched, or its constructor re-trained. Thus, improvement is priced at the size of the workflow rather than of the fault, and every step that already succeeds is paid for twice (Hwang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Dang et al., 2025). Together, these leave both challenges of 2 open: building workflow well under uncertainty and improving one at lower cost. Worse still, neither is put at risk: the tasks these systems are measured on are largely ones single competent agent already handles (Zhou et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026; Choi et al., 2025). INFLOWOP answers these in two stages (3), pricing every choice in one currency that needs no labels: how well an agents competence meets what part of the work demands, weighed against how much that agent takes to run. In the first stage, COALESCE decomposes the task to its finest parts and find the proper granularity through coalescing (3.1). In the second stage, INFLOWOP performs in-flow dynamic optimization by turning the same currency on the flow as it runs, identifying and correcting subtasks locally without losing the execution progress (3.2). One label-free cost thus serves the workflow both as it is built and as it runs. To sum up, our main contributions are: 1 COALESCE: the decomposition granularity is priced, not presumed. cost-driven bidirectional workflow construction approach (Alg. 3) over the agents on hand settles how finely the task is divided, enabling agent creation only when no available agent clears competence bar (3.1). 2 INFLOWOP: optimization in flow, without supervision. We propose INFLOWOP (Alg. 1), two-stage training-free framework that leverages COALESCE to build workflows and optimizes them in-flow (Alg. 4), without any reference answer, graded outcome, or trained assessor (3.2). 3 BRAID: benchmark for reasoning over agent-interdependent divisions. Workflow-level tasks are those single agent cannot solve effectively (C). This is the premise that motivates workflows in the first place, yet one that existing benchmarks seldom satisfy (C.1). We introduce BRAID (4), workflow-level benchmark that requires multi-agent coordinations beyond single-agent competence. 4 Evaluation: gains across domains and backbones. Our evaluation across eight domains, six backbones, and four workflow constructors shows that INFLOWOP improves over single agent from +7.15% to +11.97% under matched turn budget, and outperforms workflows baselines by up to +9.64% (5).

sections.content: When tackling complex tasks that cannot be resolved by single agent, we build multi-agent workflows: The problem. task is addressed using pool of specialist agents = {a1, . . . , am}. An LLM-powered workflow constructor produces workflow = D(Q, A) that orchestrates agents from A. The workflow is then executed to evaluate its performance Perf(W ) [0, 1] against the reference answer of Q. The objective is to maximize Perf at minimal cost via the flow Perf. However, this is affected by (1) : how is constructed, and (2) Perf: how Perf is optimized (3). 2 Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: INFLOWOP for In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization Problem Formulation Pool-Aware Workflow Construction: Given task and pool of specialist agents, automatically assemble multi-agent workflow that solves the task both effectively and efficiently. 1 Effective to solve (reliability). workflow is expected to reliably produce the correct final answer. When composing many agents, its reliability is bounded by each agents progress. 2 Efficient to run (execution). more complex task calls for more complex workflow, accordingly more subtasks, agents, and latency to run. So the complexity of workflow should be matched to the task, spending no more than the task demands. 3 Efficient to improve (optimization). When the workflow falls short, improving it should be cheap, without the time and compute of full re-execution, re-search, or model training. Building Workflow under Uncertainty. Specialist agents in the pool differ markedly in competence, thus binding subtask to an ill-suited agent is primary source of failure (Liu et al., 2025; Madhwal et al., 2026; Su et al., 2026). constructor that composes agents without regard to their fit therefore produces unreliable workflows. On the other hand, the agent pool is also finite and may hold no agent well-suited to its assigned work. This induces new agent creation rather than forcing poor fit, while at the added cost of specifying and instantiating it (Zhang et al., 2025c; Wu et al., 2025; Shang et al., 2025). Nevertheless, even well-matched agent is not guaranteed to succeed: whether it completes its assigned work correctly is uncertain, and that uncertainty surfaces only once the workflow runs, which is why fault attribution is studied on completed executions (Chae et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026a; Lin et al., 2026). Execution alone is not conclusive either, as step that satisfies what it declares can still mislead the steps that follow (D.4). Collectively, these raise the first core challenge of workflow construction: how to build good workflow under uncertainty? The Cost of Workflow Optimization. Once workflow runs, execution finally reveals which steps falter. However, acting on such evidence is expensive. The naive remedy is to re-execute the workflow or re-search over set of candidate workflows, while discarding everything already computed and progressed (Hwang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025b; Yoon et al., 2026). An increment of quality thereby charges additional full execution  (Fig. 9)  . Worse still, it presumes supervision signal absent at inference: no ground-truth answer is available to say what went wrong or where to improve. On the other hand, more targeted way is post-training, guiding to learn on success cases via supervised finetuning or improve via reward signals through reinforcement learning (Li et al., 2026; Peng et al., 2026; Nielsen et al., 2026; Dang et al., 2025). Whereas the time and computation cost of data preparation and model training can go far beyond test-time re-execution. These studies reveal the second core challenge on workflow optimization: how to improve workflow at lower cost? Agent Card Every agent is represented to the estimator by card, the sole evidence an atom is scored against (1) declared competence: written brief of what the agent is designed for, including its role, domain, and the skills and tools it commands; and (2) self-evolving empirical profile: the record an agent accumulates through execution, profiling which kinds of work it has realized successfully and where it has faltered. So declared competence is progressively complemented by one that is observed. 3 INFLOWOP: THE FLOW AS BUILT, THE FLOW AS RUN How to build reliable workflow, and optimize it at low cost (2)? Rather than relying on costly training or sampling, we cast both questions as minimizing single measurable, annotation-free surrogate: the workflows cost, which couples its reliability of success with its latency to run. As such, we minimize this cost in two stages (D.1): (1) decomposition-aware workflow construction (3.1) constructs low-cost workflow before execution, and (2) in-flow dynamic optimization (3.2) tempers it adaptively during execution. sections.title: 4 BRAID: BENCHMARK REASONING OVER AGENT-INTERDEPENDENT DIVISIONS
sections.content: Benchmark construction. workflow earns its necessity only where single agent cannot handle the task alone, yet workflows are largely measured on suites one competent agent already solves (C.1). BRAID closes this gap by composing each task at different complexity levels via two composition methods: distributed composition gives every question its own gold source, while anchored composition shares one gold source across all provides sources. We enforce four quality-control criteria, and task failing any of them is never written (C.2). Built on 10 public datasets, BRAID spans 19 evaluation-only arms across 8 domains (Tab. 3). Evaluation metrics. BRAID grades every question separately according to its answer type, so the accuracy of task is the mean score over its questions and the accuracy of BRAID dataset is the mean over its tasks (C.3). Our rubric evaluation metrics cover answer types spanning numeric, mathematical, textual, multiple-choice, list, and coding answers. 8 Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: INFLOWOP for In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization Figure 3: Evaluation on All Eight Domains of BRAID. Mean accuracy (%) per domain for the three models evaluated on the whole benchmark. Each row shows domain under the two baselines and INFLOWOP (5.1). The horizontal axis is accuracy (%). Tab. 1 covers the five domains every model is evaluated on.

sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 5.1 EXPERIMENT SETUP Setup. We compare six systems under the same pool of agents. (1) Single LLM answers task in one model call, without any tools or skills1. (2) Single agent answers with the full tools and skills provided. The remaining four construct workflows: (3) greedy-search and (4) COALESCE build workflows respectively, and our comparison between them isolates what the decomposition alone contributes. (5) COALESCE + in-flow adds the tempering of 3.2, and (6) the full method further scores each agent on the self-evolving profile, rather than on its card alone. Models. We evaluate two open-source models, Qwen3.5 (4B and 9B) (Team, 2026), together with four close-source models, GPT-5-mini (OpenAI, 2025), GPT-5.4-mini (OpenAI, 2026b), GPT-5.4 (OpenAI, 2026a), GPT-5.6-luna (OpenAI, 2026c). Data. We evaluate on BRAID (4), covering 19 evaluation arms over 14 BRAID datasets adapted from 10 public datasets across 8 domains (Tab. 3). Each is constructed at two complexity levels and two compositions dataset supports2. 5.2 WHAT THE FLOW EARNS AND WHAT EARNS THE FLOW Consistent gains across domains and backbones. INFLOWOP improves every backbone over both singleLLM and single-agent baselines (Tab. 1), achieving gains up to +21.90% over the single LLM baseline, and up to +11.97% over the single agent baseline with matched compute budget (E). What the two baselines earn depends on the backbone, as the single agent gains from +6.90% to +14.15% over the single LLM. On the other hand, what INFLOWOP earns varies by 3.74% across six backbones. The gain also exceeds what larger backbone delivers: under INFLOWOP, Qwen3.5-4B reaches 20.81%, above the single-agent accuracy of Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-5-mini, and GPT-5.4-mini. Meanwhile, the strongest backbone GPT-5.6-luna also improves from 41.99% to 49.37%. Also, the same improvement trends hold consistently on slides, science, and code, the three additional domains for the three backbones evaluated on the whole benchmark  (Fig. 3)  . Gains come not from dividing the task, but from how it is divided. Comparing against the single agent baseline evaluated on the same BRAID arms (Tab. 2), workflow constructed greedily obtains 15.49%, falling below the single-agents 17.38%. Therefore, dividing task is not by itself what earns the gain. Deciding the division by cost reverses that: COALESCE reaches 22.21%, +6.72% above greedy search and +4.83% above the single-agent baseline. In-flow tempering adds further +1.59%, and scoring each agent on the evolving profile improves +1.33% more. Each module therefore earns its place, and the two (3)-(4) optimizing in-flow earn less than the one deciding the workflow before it runs. 5.3 WHAT IMPROVES THE FLOW AND WHAT WEIGHS ON IT Cost is better computed than judged. INFLOWOP prices the cost matrix with rubric estimator to match atom demands against agent capabilities (3.1). This cost matrix can also be priced by an LLM that judges matching scores among agents for each atom in one pass. We ablate our rubric estimator against the LLM counterpart. As shown in Fig. 4 (left), the LLM estimator loses 3.27% points on Qwen3.5-4B and 3.85% on Qwen3.5-9B, leaving Qwen3.5-9B below the 22.21% it reaches under COALESCE alone (Tab. 2). Both estimators are given the same agent cards, evolving profiles, and atom demands. Therefore, what separates them is not what they know, but whether their estimated cost can effectively guide atom matching and coalescing to construct better workflows. Figure 4: How Fit Is Scored, and Where Fault Is Sought. Mean accuracy (%) on Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B. Left: using rubric estimator against an LLM for cost estimation. Right: in-flow optimization looking where contract breaches, against the same with the global pass enabled beside it (D.5). Dynamic cost matrix that updates during COALESCE guides workflow construction better. Different from dynamic cost matrix that adaptively update with newly created agents, static cost matrix is constructed once and then stays fixed. This leaves every new agent COALESCE creates outside the matching with other atoms in static matrix. As shown in Fig. 5, INFLOWOP with dynamic matrix outperforms the static matrix counterpart by +3.15% on Qwen3.5-4B and +2.55% on Qwen3.5-9B. Therefore, cost matrix dynamic evolving with the agent pool is able to more effectively guide COALESCE to find more proper granularities. 10 Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: INFLOWOP for In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization Pools that dynamically grow build better workflows. The two pools differ where no available agent fits an atom well: static agent pool settles for the closest agent it happens to hold, while dynamic agent pool creates the specialist that atom demands. As shown in Fig. 5, INFLOWOP with dynamic pool outperforms its static counterpart by +4.49% on Qwen3.5-4B and +3.29% on Qwen3.5-9B. Therefore, the pool sets ceiling that no coalescing can lift: where no available agent covers an atom, dividing the task differently only relocates the shortfall, whereas creating the missing specialist removes it. Evolving profiles help only when they remember success. An agent can be scored on its agent card alone, or on the card together with the evolving profile it accumulates. As shown in Fig. 6, profile evolving within single run gains +2.54%, +1.33%, and +2.23% over the agent card alone on Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and GPT-5.4-mini, respectively. When continuously evolving it into later runs, INFLOWOP gains further +1.21%, +1.19%, and +1.30% when only successful ones are kept. Applying all to profiles instead reaches 17.34%, 21.52%, and 26.53% respectively for three backbones, below the agent card alone on all three backbones. This indicates that what makes profile worth evolving is evidence of what an agent can do: success tells the estimator what to trust that agent with, whereas failure marks only where it once fell short, and prices the agent no better than no profile provided. Mean accuracy (%) over an agent scored (1) on its card alone, (2) on profile evolving within run, and (3) on profile evolving across runs, keeping either successful ones only or all of them. Global localization rarely fires, and loses accuracy when it does. Beyond local in-flow optimization, can workflow be improved further by global pass over the same cost matrix (D.5)? To investigate this, we compare accuracy under local-only in-flow optimization against local+global. As shown in Fig. 4 (right), enabling the global pass beside the local one yields 1.63% on Qwen3.5-4B and 1.41% on Qwen3.5-9B. This reveals that breached contract already points at what to temper, and that tempering beyond it costs more than it recovers. This finding is also the empirical evidence for our configuration, under which in-flow optimization stays local in every other experiment.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSIONS
sections.content: In this work, we present INFLOWOP (3), two-stage framework (D.1) of bidirectional decompositionaware construction (3.1) and in-flow dynamic optimization (3.2). Given the challenge of workflow-level evaluation, we contribute BRAID, benchmark whose tasks demand multi-agent coordination beyond singleagent capability (4). We evaluate INFLOWOP across eight domains and six backbones (5.1) against single-model and workflow baselines (5.2) and ablate its design choices (5.3). 11 Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: INFLOWOP for In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization

sections.title: A RELATED WORK
sections.content: A.1 WORKFLOW CONSTRUCTION OVER AN AGENT POOL Compared to hand-designed multi-agent systems that fix the roles and their order in advance (Hong et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2026), automatic construction searches for the effective structure rather than authoring it, within design space of operators, connections, or collaboration structures enumerated in advance (Zhang et al., 2025b; Zhao et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025a). That design space, rather than the agent pool, settles how finely the task is divided: prompted decomposition takes its grain from exemplars or instructions (Liu et al., 2025; Madhwal et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2023b), while plan-then-assign pipelines fix the parts before choosing which agent runs each one (Shen et al., 2023; Dong et al., 2026; Kapoor et al., 2026). Where the grain adapts, it adapts to the query alone (Su et al., 2026), or revises division already proposed (Prasad et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). Cost enters some of these decisions, in recent work alongside how far the task is divided (Zhang et al., 2025a; Cui et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026), but the quantity that prices choice is fitted before the task and refitted whenever the set of available operators changes. Which agent carries out each part divides along second axis. Some methods search over pool they leave fixed, so part that no agent fits well still goes to the closest one available (Zhuge et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2025). Another line of work adds agents that the pool does not hold, so the same part instead yields an agent created for it (Zhang et al., 2025c; Wu et al., 2025). Where system offers both, it alternates between them or settles the choice by test of similarity, rather than weighing one against the other (Shang et al., 2025; Gupta et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). As for pricing, where it appears, it ranges over backbone models rather than over reuse and creation (Yang et al., 2025a). What is missing is single price over the pool as it stands, charged per part before execution, under which creating an agent is one option inside the same search that sets the grain. A.2 OPTIMIZING WORKFLOW AFTER EXECUTION Recent work optimizes workflow performance in different ways. One route improves workflow by training: the constructor or planner is fine-tuned against scored outcomes (Li et al., 2026; Peng et al., 2026; Nielsen et al., 2026; Dang et al., 2025). Step-level signals are obtained the same way, with process reward models and learned verifiers fitted on annotated steps or on rollouts graded against known answers (Zhang et al., 2026b; Chae et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026a). Improvement is therefore paid for before the task arrives, in data and compute. second route requires no training but re-runs instead, sampling the workflow repeatedly, searching for better one, or re-executing after failure (Hwang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025b; Yoon et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026b). Each increment of quality costs another execution of the entire workflow, while what needs correcting is only small part of it. third route is both training-free and label-free: the system criticizes its own output and revises it (Shi et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2025b; Ning et al., 2026; Wan et al., 2026). Yet what it revises is the flow output, without identifying which part inside the flow is responsible. When blame is assigned within flow, it is scored on completed trace against annotated ground truth (Chen et al., 2026b), recovered by replaying trace that has already finished (Hou et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026), or derived from relation the domain itself makes checkable, such as whether claim follows from the sources cited for it (Hirsch et al., 2026). What is missing is fault located from single execution as it runs, with the correction confined to the part at fault, under no training, no reference answer, and no graded outcome. A.3 EVALUATING MULTI-AGENT WORKFLOWS Workflow systems are measured on the suites built for single models: mathematical reasoning, code generation, and question answering (Zhang et al., 2025b; 2026d; Yun et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026). On these, repeated sampling from one strong agent captures much of what coordination adds, and under matched budgets coordinating team can fall behind the same models working alone (Ann et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026; Choi 21 Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: INFLOWOP for In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization et al., 2025; Jwalapuram et al., 2026). benchmark that one agent already solves cannot show what dividing the work contributes. Benchmarks that do stress coordination exist, built around long-horizon tool use, siloed state, or distributed evidence (Gao et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c; Chen et al., 2026a). In these, the need to divide is imposed by the environment rather than arising from what the task demands: state is partitioned, tools are split between agents, or knowledge is withheld from one of them. What is missing is benchmark whose tasks require the division on their own terms, with parts that call for different competences and result that depends on how those parts combine.

sections.title: B LIMITATIONS
sections.content: INFLOWOP is evaluated on BRAID, whose tasks span eight domains and are graded against reference answer for each question (4). Tasks settled by no checkable answer, such as open-ended generation or long-horizon interaction with stateful environment, lie outside this study. In future work, we plan to extend INFLOWOP to such settings and different domains. We also plan to investigate workflows whose agents act on an environment that changes as they run. WHERE WORKFLOW BECOMES NECESSARY: BRAID FOR WORKFLOW-LEVEL

sections.title: EVALUATION
sections.content: What workflow contributes is coordination, especially how the work is divided among agents and how those divisions depend on one another. Therefore, measuring the contribution of workflow requires complex tasks whose demands exceed what one agent can meet. However, existing benchmarks rarely supply such task complexity: their tasks are simple enough for one competent agent to solve alone. Consequently, workflow evaluated on them is measured on tasks that require neither task decomposition nor multi-agent coordination beyond single-agent competence (1, A.3, C.1). To close this gap, we propose BRAID, benchmark for workflow-level agent-interdependent reasoning ([Xuehang] cite section4 data section after adding in main paper). Concretely, BRAID composes every task through two composition methods under quality control (C.2), and measures the effectiveness of workflow by the mean accuracy over the questions each task comprises (C.3). C.1 WHY WORKFLOW-LEVEL EVALUATION IS NECESSARY When workflow earns its necessity. workflow is worth building only where single agent cannot effectively carry the task alone, yet workflows are seldom evaluated on tasks that reach such complexity (1, A.3). As shown in Fig. 7, we conduct preliminary test on this gap, comparing single agent solving the task in one pass with workflow an LLM constructs for the same task: when evaluated on the original data, the single agent is more accurate than the workflow (12.02%) with notably lower cost (6.91). Therefore, coordination is not necessity for simple tasks, and running multi-agent workflows on them can further incur several times the cost. On the other hand, with BRAID composition (C.2), the ordering reverses: the single agent degrades significantly on such complex tasks, while the workflow, running under matched compute budget, showcases the strength of task decomposition and multi-agent coordination with better performance. Workflow-level task complexity is therefore necessity for workflow evaluation, and the objective BRAID targets. 22 Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: INFLOWOP for In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization Figure 7: Workflow Earns Its Necessity Only Where One Agent Falls Short. The shaded band marks the gap between the two solvers in accuracy (left) and in cost (right). Cost is counted in units of one single-agent run on the original data, and on BRAID the two solvers run under matched budgets. Both use gpt-5-mini over 150 samples of SlideVQA (doc variant of BRAID), Distributed at complexity level = 5. Why workflow-level evaluation is necessary. The benchmarks multi-agent workflow is usually measured on sit on the left side of each subplot (Fig. 7: left original half of both subplots): single competent agent is already able to solve their tasks, which therefore demand neither task decomposition nor coordination among agents. As result, evaluating workflow on them cannot effectively measure how workflow performs and what it actually contributes. Instead, reliable workflow-level evaluation requires tasks whose complexity demands multi-agent coordination beyond single-agent capability. C.2 BENCHMARKING WORKFLOW-LEVEL EVALUATION BRAID constructs workflow-level tasks by composing each task with questions and providing extra sources beyond those its questions require, without stating which source serves which question. We use to denote the complexity level of task. Answering one task therefore demands both halves of what workflow is for: dividing the task, and reaching its answers through coordinated routing. Here, we define routing as locating the source question is answered from and reasoning over it to that questions answer. We use solver to denote an evaluated system in general: single LLM, an agent, or multi-agent workflow that receives the task and produces its answers. Composition methods. task is composed in one of two methods: distributed or anchored. source here is one document or image provided with the task, however many files it takes to provide it, and the source question is answered from is its gold source. They differ in where the gold sources of tasks questions sit and therefore in what the division and the routing each demand: 1 Distributed: every question has its own source. Each distributed task takes questions that are each answered from different source. BRAID provides those sources, and additionally inputs (k 1) more sources that answer none of the questions, which we call distractors. As result, distributed task inputs (2k 1) sources in total. Distractors come from inside BRAID, and the kind of input decides which extra sources supply them. dataset whose inputs are documents draws its distractors from its own split, so distractor is the same kind of document as the gold source and differs only in what it contains. dataset whose inputs are images draws from different dataset of the same kind, which keeps routing real via strict quality control while ensuring that gold sources own family never supplies distractor (Alg. 2). dataset whose items provide no input of their own draws its distractors from charts. The draw is randomly seeded and prefers the least-used sources of the split, so no source dominates the benchmark and the same composition is reproduced on every rebuild. Quality control. source counts as distractor only if it answers no question of the task: when any other provided source also answers question, that question has more than one gold source, and thus the task can no longer isolate the routing it is built to evaluate. BRAID therefore rejects such tasks while composing them (Alg. 2) rather than filtering them after construction, and task that fails any of the four criteria below is never written. (1) Separation keeps no provided source standing in for another: two questions of one task do not rest on near-duplicate gold sources, and distractor resembling any of the tasks gold sources is redrawn. (2) Routing requires each question to mention at least one word or phrase that appears in its own gold source and in no other provided source, so that the question can identify that source among those provided. (3) Leakage forbids any source other than questions gold source from containing that questions answer. (4) Answerability covers what text matching cannot decide: where task supplies images or documents, an LLM judges every pairing of question with provided source, and the task is discarded if any questions answer holds against source other than its gold source. D.4 STEP IS WORTH WHAT IT LEADS TO The Verdict Lies Downstream, Not in the Middle Whether an intermediate output helps or harms cannot be determined from that output alone. step may satisfy the conditions it is expected to meet yet still steer the flow wrong, while it may also violate them yet still bridge the flow to the correct final answer. The sign of deviation is thus settled by where it drives the rest of the flow, not by the step where it appears or by what that step produces. Therefore, no local judgment of that step, however it is computed, recovers it. Figure 8 shows one such case: the subtask asks which images carry particular set of information, so its declared condition is that the output identify the useful ones. Before tempering, the agent names two images with wrong evidence but successfully meeting that condition. Thus, neither image carries the information the subtask demands, and the flow continues on wrong evidence that misleads its final answer. After tempering, the agent responds that no image contains what is required. That answer violates the condition, yet it is the accurate one. Consequently, the flow carries on with it and reaches the correct final answer. However, if scored against its declared condition, the step that helped is recorded as the step that failed. We therefore judge every temper by the outcome of the flow it belongs to, without relying on step-level assessment. step-level metric is not reliable or stricter measure of the same quantity, as on cases of this kind it carries the opposite sign. However, workflow may nonetheless terminate without usable answer for cause lying several steps upstream, without violating local contract. Rather than fall back on global re-search, we extend in-flow optimization with an optional global localization: the temper stays local, and only where to look becomes global. Once the local pass ends without usable answer, the whole graph is scanned to rank subtasks by suspicion: susp(si) = (cid:0)1 ˆpi (cid:1)(cid:0)1 + Desc(si)(cid:1) + 1[si flagged] (22) where subtask already flagged by local detection receives an additive bonus. Global localization therefore buys only where to look at the final failure, while every correction is committed locally. It is disabled in all main experiments, and we evaluate it as an ablation (5.3).
